topic.title: The seat lottery home
topic.claim: Every city runs on people who go home twice a year, and for them the station isn't a journey, it's a holding pen.
topic.behaviour: Workers from Delhi heading to Bihar and UP for Chhath wait in holding areas, and platform entry is limited to people with confirmed tickets. The system plans for the rush like it is an emergency, even though it comes every year.
topic.mechanism: Trains are added late and temporary fixes get reused each season. A rush that happens on the same dates every year is still managed like a surprise.
topic.group: Migrant workers and their friends in metros, who go home only for the big festivals
topic.moment: You open the ticket app at 8 am the day booking opens, and every train home already shows a waiting list.

turn.believed: Festival crowds are a one-time rush that the railways handle as best they can.
turn.actually: The rush is on the calendar every year, and the fix is still a waiting area outside the platform.

topic.feeling: Taken for granted by the city I work for
topic.villain: A transport system that handles a predictable annual rush with temporary arrangements
topic.because: Adding permanent capacity for two peak weeks is expensive, so crowd control is cheaper than seats. The people who bear the cost have no way to push back.

proof.fact: Platform tickets are suspended from 3 to 14 November at six Delhi stations, and a permanent holding area outside Platform 16 at New Delhi can hold about 7,000 people.

topic.payoff: The city counts on you to leave on those dates, and it still isn't ready when you do.
topic.send_to: A colleague who is leaving for Chhath and has no confirmed seat
real_details: A second holding area was commissioned at Anand Vihar Terminal this year
topic.news_peg: Platform tickets suspended at six Delhi stations from 3 to 14 November (2026-11-03) and Chhath holding areas (2026-11-09)
topic.why_now: Chhath travel is happening right now.

score.why: The waiting list and the holding pen for the trip home are lived by millions every Diwali and Chhath. The turn is that the city counts on you leaving and still isn't ready.

notes: The take's premise is wrong: The central mechanism fails. It says railways use cheap crowd control (the platform ticket ban and the permanent holding area) instead of adding capacity. Railways actually did both. For this season, Northern Railway raised Chhath special trains from about 400 last year to 650 and added roughly 25% more coaches, with festive special trips nationally in the thousands. The premise that extra trains 'sit idle the rest of the year' is also wrong about how this works. Festival specials mostly run on spare or reassigned coaches and extra coaches added to regular trains, not on a dedicated fleet parked for 50 weeks. The factual premises do hold: platform ticket sales were suspended from 3 to 14 November at six Delhi stations, and a permanent holding area for about 7,000 people now sits outside Platform 16 at New Delhi, replacing the temporary tents used before. The 7,000 figure appears in only one or two reports.. How it actually works: Indian Railways handles the Chhath peak mainly by adding capacity. It notifies festival special trains, which are announced in stages from about September through the festival itself, using rakes moved over from other routes and zones. It also adds extra coaches to regular services. This year Northern Railway put the count at 650 specials, up from about 400. Demand (footfall up about 25–30%) still runs ahead of the number of trains the busy Delhi–Bihar/UP lines can carry, so waitlists remain. Crowd measures like the platform ticket ban and the permanent holding area are added on top of the extra trains, not used in their place. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

_ledger.text:
[cover] Chhath comes every year. [The station acts surprised] every time.
The dates never change. Neither does the scramble at the gate.
 

[slide 1] Chhath comes on the same dates every year. Delhi's stations still handle it like a surprise.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] You open the ticket app at 8 am, the moment booking opens. Every train to Patna, Darbhanga and Gorakhpur already shows a waiting list.
So you book the waitlist anyway and refresh like it's a second job.

[slide 3] The special trains get added late, so you plan your leave around a ticket that may never confirm.

[slide 4] This year the fix was a rule. From 3 to 14 November, six Delhi stations stopped selling platform tickets. If you're not travelling, you mostly don't get in.

[slide 5] Your friend can't walk you to the coach anymore. At New Delhi, a permanent holding area outside Platform 16 takes about 7,000 people at a time.

[slide 6] Inside, you stand with your bags and guess. The platform number gets announced to a crowd that can't even see the board.

[slide 7] Extra trains and tracks for two peak weeks are expensive, and they sit idle the rest of the year. A waiting area is cheap.
And the people stuck in it can't complain. They're on a train out by then.

[slide 8] Sure, a holding area beats a crush on the stairs. Nobody's arguing with that.
But look at the word permanent. The one thing built to last is the place you wait.

[slide 9] The city knows exactly who leaves. The guard at your gate asks for leave a month early. You blocked that week on the team calendar in September.
Offices, kitchens and building sites sorted out that week ages ago.

[slide 10] Your manager has your Chhath dates in September.
The station meets you in November with a holding pen.

[end card] Come back to this the morning booking opens for next year's Chhath trains.
Send to the colleague leaving for Chhath this week who still has no confirmed seat.

[caption] Chhath train rush comes on fixed dates, and the one permanent fix is a place to stand and wait.

Seats for two weeks cost money all year. A waiting area costs little, and the people in it are gone before anyone asks.

"Confirm hua?" is the only question anyone at the office asks that week.

Send this to the colleague leaving for Chhath this week who is still refreshing a waitlisted ticket.

[alt text] A text post in ten slides. It argues that the Chhath rush from Delhi comes on the same dates every year, yet railways handle it with temporary fixes: waitlisted trains on booking day, special trains added late, platform tickets suspended from 3 to 14 November at six Delhi stations, and a permanent holding area outside Platform 16 at New Delhi for about 7,000 people. It explains that a waiting area is cheaper than extra trains, and that the travellers stuck in it have already left the city by the time they could complain. It credits the holding area for preventing crushes but points out the only permanent thing built is a place to wait, while offices and homes plan months ahead around workers going home.

cover.headline: Chhath comes every year. [The station acts surprised] every time.
cover.sub: The dates never change. Neither does the scramble at the gate.

paragraphs: Chhath comes on the same dates every year. Delhi's stations still handle it like a surprise.
slides.why_swipe: If everyone knows the dates, why does it still feel like a scramble?

paragraphs: You open the ticket app at 8 am, the moment booking opens. Every train to Patna, Darbhanga and Gorakhpur already shows a waiting list.
So you book the waitlist anyway and refresh like it's a second job.
slides.why_swipe: Whose fault is the waitlist, really?

paragraphs: The special trains get added late, so you plan your leave around a ticket that may never confirm.
slides.why_swipe: So what does the system actually prepare instead of seats?

paragraphs: This year the fix was a rule. From 3 to 14 November, six Delhi stations stopped selling platform tickets. If you're not travelling, you mostly don't get in.
Your friend can't walk you to the coach anymore. At New Delhi, a permanent holding area outside Platform 16 takes about 7,000 people at a time.
Inside, you stand with your bags and guess. The platform number gets announced to a crowd that can't even see the board.
slides.why_swipe: Why build a waiting area instead of more trains?

paragraphs: Extra trains and tracks for two peak weeks are expensive, and they sit idle the rest of the year. A waiting area is cheap.
And the people stuck in it can't complain. They're on a train out by then.
slides.why_swipe: Is the holding area at least an improvement?

paragraphs: Sure, a holding area beats a crush on the stairs. Nobody's arguing with that.
But look at the word permanent. The one thing built to last is the place you wait.
slides.why_swipe: And who exactly is being made to wait?

paragraphs: The city knows exactly who leaves. The guard at your gate asks for leave a month early. You blocked that week on the team calendar in September.
Offices, kitchens and building sites sorted out that week ages ago.
slides.why_swipe: So if the city plans for it, why doesn't the station?

paragraphs: Your manager has your Chhath dates in September.
The station meets you in November with a holding pen.

end.save: Come back to this the morning booking opens for next year's Chhath trains.
end.send: Send to the colleague leaving for Chhath this week who still has no confirmed seat.

draft.alt_text: A text post in ten slides. It argues that the Chhath rush from Delhi comes on the same dates every year, yet railways handle it with temporary fixes: waitlisted trains on booking day, special trains added late, platform tickets suspended from 3 to 14 November at six Delhi stations, and a permanent holding area outside Platform 16 at New Delhi for about 7,000 people. It explains that a waiting area is cheaper than extra trains, and that the travellers stuck in it have already left the city by the time they could complain. It credits the holding area for preventing crushes but points out the only permanent thing built is a place to wait, while offices and homes plan months ahead around workers going home.

claims.text: From 3 to 14 November, six Delhi stations stopped selling platform tickets.
If you're not travelling, you mostly don't get onto the platforms (only confirmed passengers are ordinarily allowed).
A permanent holding area outside Platform 16 at New Delhi takes about 7,000 people at a time.

draft.caption:
Chhath train rush comes on fixed dates, and the one permanent fix is a place to stand and wait.

Seats for two weeks cost money all year. A waiting area costs little, and the people in it are gone before anyone asks.

"Confirm hua?" is the only question anyone at the office asks that week.

Send this to the colleague leaving for Chhath this week who is still refreshing a waitlisted ticket.
